blueprint_topic: Management of Care — financial barriers to cancer-treatment adherence, interdisciplinary communication, and support-resource referral
stem: A client receiving oral cancer therapy tells the nurse, 'Even with insurance, the copay is so high that I have been skipping some doses to make the prescription last longer.' Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Recognize the cost barrier, communicate the missed doses to the oncology team, and connect the client with financial-navigation or assistance resources.
options.B: Because the client has insurance, treat the skipped doses mainly as an adherence problem and reinforce the prescribed schedule before exploring financial support.
options.C: Recommend taking fewer doses on expensive weeks to extend the prescription, then returning to the prescribed schedule after financial assistance is arranged.
options.D: Start with an insurance appeal and postpone discussion of the missed doses with the oncology team until the next visit, because the prescription has not changed.

rationale: A is correct. NCI defines financial toxicity as cost-related financial problems and states that copayments and coinsurance can cause financial toxicity even for people with cancer who have health insurance. NCI specifically documents skipping doses or taking less medicine than prescribed to make a prescription last longer because of cost. NCI also advises clients to tell the health care team when costs may be a burden, notes that the team needs to know how costs are affecting the client, and describes financial counselors, social workers, financial navigators, and medication-assistance resources as potential sources of help. B is incorrect because active insurance does not rule out financial toxicity and labeling the behavior primarily as an adherence problem misses the stated cost barrier. C is incorrect because intentionally reducing prescribed doses perpetuates the cost-related nonadherence identified by NCI rather than following the prescribed medicine schedule. D is incorrect because the missed doses are already affecting treatment adherence; deferring communication with the oncology team leaves an active treatment problem unaddressed while financial support is pursued.
educational_objective: Recognize cost-related medication underuse as financial toxicity and respond by communicating the adherence problem to the cancer-care team while coordinating financial-navigation, social-work, or medication-assistance resources.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the original extreme correct-answer length cue and absolute-word distractors. The final options distinguish appropriate recognition/communication/resource coordination from three realistic errors: dismissing financial toxicity because insurance exists, endorsing cost-driven dose reduction, and delaying communication of an active adherence problem while pursuing an insurance process.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly integrates NCI-supported recognition of cost-related nonadherence, communication with the cancer-care team, and referral to financial-navigation/assistance resources.
option_audit.B: Plausible compliance-framing error; incorrect because NCI states that insured clients can still experience financial toxicity and the disclosed cost barrier is clinically relevant to adherence.
option_audit.C: Plausible self-rationing strategy; incorrect because NCI identifies taking less medicine than prescribed to stretch a prescription as cost-related nonadherence and separately advises following the prescribed medicine schedule.
option_audit.D: Plausible administrative-first response; incorrect because delaying communication leaves already-missed cancer-therapy doses unaddressed while financial assistance is sought.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on only/none/all/always/never/must-type distractor absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are closely balanced (A 152, B 162, C 157, D 161 characters); the key is not the longest.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are parallel nursing responses combining adherence, cost, team communication, or resource-navigation decisions.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified in the pre-stage audit; B, C, and D each leave a source-supported component of the active problem mishandled. Post-fetch adversarial reread remains required.
